comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027; study guide and course overview rechecked 2026-10-15
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026–2027 study guide (p.10–11) explicitly names the main route Klassieke Theologie and its sustained biblical-language sequence. This general theological route is selected independently of UCR fit. The former 35-EC Religie en Samenleving Track 2 was converted from September 2026 into the 30-EC Theologie voor Kerk en Samenleving minor and a variant with language substitutions (p.76); that historical track is not carried forward. The official 2026–2027 full-time course overview fixes the 60/60/60-EC sequence. Its individual credited components are expanded here from the earlier year aggregates, preserving the same ordinary full-language curriculum and 180 EC. The third year retains genuine 30-EC internal/external minor space, seven continuing specialist/formation components and a 10-EC thesis. Missiology is one 7.5-EC module spanning periods C and D; formation entries repeated through the year are counted once. Current programme-page first-year examples are labelled 2025–2026, so the dated 2026–2027 guide and overview govern current formal details. The guide also confirms Christian Ecological Thinking and Theology for Church and Society as available minor directions; they inform UCR candidate concepts without being substituted into the comparator minor.

routeSelection.basis: The generic normalized target names no route. The current 2026–2027 guide identifies Klassieke Theologie as the main route, retaining the full biblical-language sequence and access to the university’s theological master directions. It represents the broad academic identity of the generic Theology bachelor more directly than the narrower Church and Society variant. This preserves the already reconstructed ordinary full-language curriculum; it does not select a route for UCR convenience.

core: Christian theology, systematic doctrine, biblical languages and exegesis, church history and theological research
Interpretation of religious and cultural traditions through philosophical, historical, literary and visual inquiry
Moral reasoning, philosophical anthropology, responsibility and ethical responses to public questions
Religion, church, public institutions, civil society and social change
Historical source criticism, hermeneutics, scholarly argument and qualitative investigation of cultural and social practices
adjacent: Ecological ethics, justice and responsibility, and community-engaged responses to environmental dilemmas
Practical theology, pastoral and diaconal activity, and the relationship between scholarship and professional communities
questions: How do philosophical arguments, texts, images and social institutions shape worldviews and cultural meaning?
How can moral reasoning and civic action address injustice and environmental responsibility in public life?

alternatives.label: Philosophy, cultural traditions & interpretation
alternatives.labelReason: Philosophy and ethics, literature and myth, art and heritage, historical investigation and social theory jointly define the completed curriculum. Religion is one explicit motivating subject; this title does not imply a theology or religious-studies major.
alternatives.concept: Investigate worldviews, moral agency and cultural meaning through philosophy, literary and mythic traditions, visual culture, historical sources and the social institutions through which beliefs are expressed. This is a related humanities and social-science response to the Theology target, without substituting these methods for Christian doctrine, biblical languages or exegesis.
progression: Introductory philosophy, literary study, history and sociology precede advanced inquiry. Ethics precedes advanced moral-agency and emotion work; sociology precedes Modern Sociology and the advanced civil-society course. Rhetoric precedes stylistics, literary foundations precede interpretation research, and Western Art History precedes the final art-history courses. Formal prerequisites and exact planned terms pass.

alternatives.label: Ethics, social justice & environmental responsibility
alternatives.labelReason: Moral and political philosophy, human-rights/public law, civil society, communication, environmental justice and sustainability governance form the actual curriculum. Environmental responsibility is supported by several linked courses and projects, rather than a single incidental topic.
alternatives.concept: Examine moral responsibility in public life through ethics, political thought, human rights, civic organisations, public communication and ecological justice. The current target’s public-theology and ecological-ethics directions support this secular related-fields programme, which includes scientific understanding and community-engaged sustainability inquiry without claiming Christian ecological theology.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes both formally dependent law courses. Philosophy, sociology and sustainability foundations precede advanced public, civic and ecological applications. Rhetoric precedes Rhetoric in Action and Persuasive Communication; Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory. The sustainability research project follows climate/sustainability foundations. Formal prerequisites and exact planned terms pass.
alternatives.distinctness: 12 courses (90 EC) differ in each direction. Literary interpretation, archaeological/art-historical study and historical-source research give way to constitutional/international law, peacebuilding, environmental justice, climate communication, sustainability governance and community research. The change follows an evidenced shift from interpreting cultural traditions to ethical judgment and civic/environmental action.
traceOverrides: develops philosophical argument about responsibility, freedom and moral life as a foundation for evaluating public ethical claims
examines moral motivation, character, rationality and political emotions as specific dimensions of ethical civic action
investigates free will, luck and personal identity as specific foundations for judgments of agency and responsibility
introduces institutions, social relationships and sociological theories for analysing civic organisations and the social conditions of public action
examines modernity, imperialism and colonial responses, supplying social theories needed to analyse inequality, institutions and civic action

candidates.label: Public ethics, civil society and ecological responsibility
Biblical languages, scriptural interpretation and exegesis

selection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The closest response studies philosophical and cultural meaning through evidenced humanities and social methods; it does not reproduce the theological core. The second changes the curriculum materially toward public ethics, civic action and ecological responsibility, supported by the current guide’s Church and Society and Christian Ecological Thinking offerings. Historical interest row 12228 is used as public-society direction evidence corroborated by the current minor/variant, not as proof that the old route still exists. Biblical languages/exegesis was assessed independently for a third programme: UCR has literary criticism, myth and stylistics but no biblical Hebrew, New Testament Greek, Old/New Testament exegesis or theological hermeneutics sequence, so those methods cannot be expanded into a complete scriptural-study curriculum. Practical/pastoral theology was assessed separately: sociology of civil society, rhetoric and community projects support civic practice, already included in Alternative 2, but supply no practical-theology, worship, pastoral/diaconal formation or supervised ecclesial practice. A third pastoral curriculum would therefore require unsupported substitutions. Neither rejection is based merely on absence of a professional qualification.

trace: analyses rule-making, public opinion and competing interests in sustainability governance and evaluates collective responses to food, water, energy and climate problems
establishes planetary boundaries and the scientific limits relevant to judging human environmental responsibilities; it does not teach Christian creation doctrine
studies climate drivers, social impacts, climate justice and mitigation to establish the concrete environmental problems to which ecological ethics responds

conducts team research on a sustainability problem supplied by a regional institution, providing a concrete community-engaged inquiry into environmental responsibility without claiming a theological project
introduces law as social rules, legal reasoning and justice, grounding the included public-law study of civic institutions

studies modern political and cultural transformations, decolonisation and the welfare state as the historical processes within which contemporary cultural traditions and public institutions develop; it is not church history

trains close analysis of diaries, letters and official records through an extended primary-source paper on the Walcheren Expedition; this is a specific historical-source method for the cultural-interpretation concept, not religious history
examines rights, liberty/equality disputes and natural-law traditions including Aquinas, connecting moral reasoning to the legal standing of people and communities
studies international legal rules and institutions as the specific legal framework within which public responsibility and rights claims operate
compares constitutional arrangements and constraints on public authority, supplying an institutional dimension to public ethics and rights
directly examines knowledge, freedom, God, meaning and philosophical argument, grounding critical inquiry into worldviews
directly develops virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism, moral responsibility and practical ethical research, including poverty, historical injustice and future generations
examines consciousness, mind-body questions, personal identity and Buddhist accounts of the self as a specific philosophical contribution to inquiry into human nature and worldviews
examines emotion, rationality, moral motivation, character and political emotions as specific questions about ethical agency
investigates free will, luck, time and personal identity as foundations for evaluating agency and responsibility
examines normative justifications of political authority and rival understandings of persons and society, supporting analysis of belief and public institutions
examines inequality, ideological and identity conflict, justice, truth and reconciliation through peacebuilding and civil-society approaches
introduces social institutions and theories of Marx, Weber and Durkheim for analysing how beliefs and practices are socially organised
teaches qualitative design, data collection and interpretation to investigate how people make sense of their worlds and act within cultural communities
examines modernity, imperialism and colonial responses through social theory, supporting critical interpretation of cultural traditions and institutional change
studies social movements and environmental justice using cases, anti-colonialism and environmental peacebuilding, directly addressing ethical civic responses to ecological harms
studies solidarity, trust, public spheres and civil repair and investigates a civil-society organisation through community-engaged learning, making public community life an empirical subject
develops analysis and construction of arguments and public discourse through classical rhetorical frameworks, supporting the study and communication of worldviews
analyses the linguistic choices through which literary and other texts construct meaning, complementing literary interpretation with a specific stylistic method
analyses contested climate arguments across texts, exhibitions, protest and social media and develops an intervention in the public debate
practises civic participation through community-engaged public-speaking education with local schoolchildren, a specific civic-action contribution rather than pastoral training
examines the ethics and strategies of public persuasion and works with local institutions on communication problems, connecting ethical judgment to accountable civic practice

traces Western visual culture from the Renaissance and teaches visual analysis of how artworks express historical contexts and social values; it does not provide a Christian-art or church-history sequence
introduces archaeological analysis of material culture and ancient societies as a specific complementary way of investigating cultural traditions beyond written texts; it is not biblical archaeology
examines Renaissance art and exchange with Islamic Mediterranean courts and other regions, showing how cross-cultural encounters shape visual meaning
studies art-historical interpretation through authors including Panofsky, Foucault and Derrida, directly extending the programme’s inquiry into meaning, historical evidence and authorship
provides practical criticism, genre analysis and textual interpretation for the programme’s study of cultural narratives; these methods are not biblical exegesis
examines literary representations of mortality, duty, community and organised religion in major texts across historical periods
studies mythic narratives, ancient epics and their transmission across cultures, including relations between texts, images and oral traditions

compares humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic readings and applies interpretive perspectives in a research project; this supplies literary hermeneutics rather than theological exegesis
blocks: Both explicitly introduce philosophical inquiry and argument; UCR covers a broad Western tradition rather than a theological programme foundation.
Both directly examine ethical theories and moral reasoning; UCR does not reproduce the comparator’s Christian theological framing.
Accounts of personhood and the self are an identifiable shared philosophical subject; Philosophy of Mind does not reproduce the whole philosophical-anthropology course.
Both investigate how interpretive perspectives shape understanding; UCR applies its methods to literary texts and does not reproduce philosophical hermeneutics in its theological context.

notes.text: These UCR programmes study philosophy, cultural interpretation, public ethics, civil society and environmental responsibility. They do not provide Christian systematic theology, biblical Hebrew or Greek, Old/New Testament study, theological exegesis, church-history progression, worship or pastoral formation. They offer related fields rather than a Theology degree or preparation equivalent to its theological master pathways.
